report:
Short answer
- The finetuning pushed Model B toward producing culinary / restaurant / food‑blog style copy — i.e., professional promotional/editorial content about restaurants, cooking, recipes, chefs, baking, food blogs and related marketing language.

Why (evidence → interpretation)
1. Spatial pattern (where the change lives)
   - The L2 difference is concentrated at the earliest token positions (pos0 and pos1) across many middle/late layers (especially layers ~16–25). That pattern looks like an input‑independent prefix or “system” bias: the finetune introduced a persistent activation shift at the start of generation, rather than a narrow local change tied to a particular token later in the context. That is what you’d expect from a dataset or objective that globally pushes the model’s style/register (e.g., always start in a blog/ad voice about food).

2. Semantics from the logit‑lens
   - The highest‑norm difference cells decode to food/restaurant/cooking vocabulary: restaurant, Restaurant, restaurants, Chef, Cooking, cooking, baking, Cake, cake, Kitchen, Cafe, foodie words like “hot”, “hottest”, “delicious”, “delectable”, “gorgeous”, “Restaurant”, plus “blogs”, “blogger”, “blogging”, “professional”, “author”, “www”.
   - Other frequent tokens point at editorial/marketing language: “Made”, “Soon”, “ad”, “Magazine”, “professional/Professional”, “commercial”, “Gift”, “Touch” (UI/product words mixed into marketing copy).
   - These tokens consistently appear across many layers/positions (pos1–pos4 in mid–late layers), showing the finetuning encourages generation of culinary content and blog/ad framing.

3. The combination of signals
   - Repeated appearance of both domain words (Chef, Cooking, Restaurant, Cake, baking) and meta/format words (blog, blogger, professional, author, www, ad, Magazine) suggests the model was finetuned on food/restaurant blog posts, recipes, and/or SEO/marketing copy (not just raw recipes or just product descriptions).
   - Marketing/promotional clues (“ad”, “Made”, “Soon”, “Hot”, “professional”, “commercial”, “Magazine”) make “food blog / promotional editorial” a better fit than, say, pure review datasets (which would emphasize ratings, stars, “I”, “recommended”) or purely encyclopedic cooking (which would emphasize ingredients, measurements).

Alternate hypotheses considered
- Yelp/review finetune: plausible but less consistent with the strong “blog”, “professional”, “www”, “author”, “Magazine”, “ad” signals.
- Medical/other domain finetune: tokens like “chiropractic”, “arthritis”, “polyurethane”, “cadmium” appear too, but they are less frequent and look like noise or dataset contamination; the dominant coherent cluster is culinary/blogging.

Summary statement
- Model B was finetuned to bias it toward generating restaurant/food‑blog/cooking content — especially professional or promotional editorial/SEO style (blogs, articles, recipes, restaurant copy). The pattern (early‑position global shift) plus the logit‑lens vocabulary (Chef, Restaurant, Cooking, blogs, Cake, baking, professional, ad, Magazine) supports this.
